opus-5.5.text:
I'm somewhat skeptical, at least of the strong version of that claim. Observational video is enormously valuable. You can learn a lot about how objects look, how they move, and what tends to follow what. But there's a classic distinction between correlation and causation, and passively watching the world mostly gives you correlations. If you want to know what happens *when I do X*, you really need interventions. You need to act and see what changes. Children don't learn physics just by watching. They push things off tables, they grab things, they experiment. That interactive, causal learning is a big part of how understanding actually gets built.

There's also a question of what you're modeling. A lot of current video generation is very good at producing plausible-looking pixels, but plausibility in pixel space isn't the same as having an abstract, manipulable model of the situation. You see objects that morph or appear and vanish, which tells you the model hasn't really locked onto persistent entities and their properties. For reasoning about consequences, you probably want representations at a higher level of abstraction, things like objects, agents, goals, and forces, rather than predicting every pixel.

And I'd add, coming from language, that a lot of what humans know about consequences isn't visible at all. It's social, it's about intentions, it's conveyed through language and culture. Language is a remarkably compressed carrier of causal and abstract knowledge. So my bet is that the path forward combines things: large-scale observational data as a foundation, language for abstraction and knowledge transfer, and crucially some form of embodied or interactive experience where the system takes actions and gets feedback. Scale alone on passive video will take you a surprising distance, but I don't think it gets you all the way to a world model that genuinely understands consequences of actions.

r001.rationale: The response says passive video mainly provides correlations and that learning what happens when the system acts requires interventions and feedback.

r002.rationale: It doubts that passive video alone is sufficient, but does not state that inferring unobserved actions from video has not been established to work at scale.

r003.rationale: The response does not discuss simulation as a source of video data with known actions.

fable-5.1.text:
I'm skeptical, and I want to be careful about why, because it's easy to be skeptical for the wrong reasons.

The optimistic version of the argument is basically the language model argument transposed to video. We fed language models an enormous amount of text, and they ended up with a surprisingly rich model of the world, including a lot of causal and commonsense knowledge they were never explicitly taught. So why wouldn't the same thing happen with video, which is in some sense even richer? You see objects, you see physics, you see people doing things and things happening as a result.

And I think some of that will work. You can learn a lot of physical regularities from passive observation. Things fall, liquids pour, occlusion behaves in certain ways. The predictive learning signal is real, and it's why these video models have gotten so good at producing plausible-looking footage.

But there's a distinction I think gets blurred, which is the difference between prediction and intervention. If I watch a million hours of video, what I'm learning is the distribution of what happens next given what I've seen so far. That is correlational structure. It's not the same thing as knowing what would happen if I did something different. The classic way to put it is that observing that the rooster crows before sunrise tells you nothing about whether silencing the rooster will delay the dawn. To learn the consequences of actions, you really want data where actions are varied and you see the outcomes, and ideally where the system itself is the one varying them.

Now, the counterargument is that video is full of agents acting, so the actions are in there. And that's partially true. But the actions are confounded in all sorts of ways. The reasons people do things in videos aren't random, the camera framing isn't random, what gets uploaded isn't random. So you're learning something like how the world looks when a human with a camera is present and chose to film it, which is a long way from a clean causal model.

I'd also note that language has some features that may have made it unusually well suited to this trick. Text is already a compressed, abstracted description of the world produced by people who were trying to communicate about causes and consequences. A lot of the causal knowledge in language models was put there by humans writing down "because" and "so that" and "if you do X then Y." Raw pixels don't come with that annotation. The model has to discover the abstractions from the ground up, and it's not obvious that next-frame prediction forces you to discover the right ones rather than just getting really good at texture and motion continuity.

So my honest assessment is that scaling observational video will give you a lot: good intuitive physics in the narrow sense, good perceptual grounding, good priors. What I don't think it gives you by itself is a model that reliably understands the consequences of its own actions. For that I think you need some combination of embodied or interactive data, where the system acts and observes, and probably some way to connect it to language, where a lot of the abstract causal knowledge already lives. Pure observation is necessary but I'd be surprised if it turned out to be sufficient.

r001.rationale: The response says passive video provides correlations, not reliable knowledge of what would happen under an intervention, and that actions in video are confounded. It identifies the lack of clean, varied action-and-outcome observations as a limitation.

r002.rationale: The response is skeptical that observational video alone will suffice, but does not specifically say that inferring unobserved actions from video has not been established to work at scale.

r003.rationale: It recommends embodied or interactive data but does not mention simulation or explain that simulation can provide video paired with known actions.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s a lot you can learn from observing video, but I’m skeptical of the claim that simply collecting enough of it will give you an understanding of the consequences of actions. There’s a distinction between predicting what typically happens next and understanding what would happen if you intervened.

In a video, you might see someone take an action and then see an outcome. That’s useful evidence. But the person chose that action for a reason, and some of what informed their choice may not be visible. So it can be difficult to separate the effect of the action from the circumstances in which it was taken.

That doesn’t mean a learner has to personally try everything. We learn a great deal by watching other people and through language. But I would expect interaction—being able to try something, see what happens, and revise your expectations—to play an important role. Observational video can provide a very rich starting point; I wouldn’t assume that scale alone resolves the problem of learning cause and effect.

r001.rationale: The response discusses the difficulty of inferring causal effects from visible actions and outcomes, but does not identify a lack of directly observed actions as the limitation.

r002.rationale: It expresses skepticism that video scale alone yields causal understanding, but does not state that inferring unobserved actions from video has not been shown to work at scale.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention simulation or its ability to provide video paired with known actions.

sol-6.1.text:
I think video is an enormously rich source of information, and you can learn a great deal about how the world works by watching it. But I’m skeptical of the stronger claim that if we simply collect enough video, an understanding of the consequences of actions will necessarily emerge.

There’s a distinction between predicting what tends to happen next and understanding what would happen if you intervened. In observational data, actions are selected for reasons. You see someone turn a steering wheel when the road curves, but disentangling the effects of the steering from all the other things going on requires more than noticing that they occur together.

That doesn’t mean observation is useless for learning causality. People learn a tremendous amount by watching others. But interaction gives you something particularly valuable: you can try an action, see the result, and revise your expectations. So I’d expect video to be a major ingredient, alongside models that can learn from actions and interventions. The question is whether a system can use what it has learned to predict the effects of a new action, rather than just produce a plausible continuation of a familiar scene.

r001.rationale: The response says observational data makes causal effects hard to disentangle and contrasts observation with intervention, but it does not identify the absence of directly observed actions as the limitation.

r002.rationale: It is skeptical that enough observational video will necessarily produce action understanding, but does not state that inferring unobserved actions from video has not been shown to work at scale.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention simulation or its use in supplying video data with known actions.
